## Summary

Across 3,420 sailings between December and February, **91.6%** departed within
two minutes of the timetable. Delays cluster on the Skerry route in the
evening, when one vessel covers two rotations (@fig-delays).

::: {.callout-note}
## Data source
Departure times come from the harbour's AIS receiver, matched to the published
timetable by vessel and route. Sailings with no position report are excluded.
:::

```{python}
#| label: setup
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sailings = pd.read_parquet("data/sailings-winter-2026.parquet")
sailings["delay"] = (sailings.actual - sailings.scheduled).dt.total_seconds() / 60
```

## Delays by route

```{python}
#| label: fig-delays
#| fig-cap: "Median delay by hour of day, per route."
#| fig-width: 7
#| echo: false
by_hour = sailings.groupby(["route", sailings.scheduled.dt.hour]).delay.median()
by_hour.unstack(0).plot(drawstyle="steps-mid")
plt.ylabel("median delay (min)")
```

| Route              | Sailings | On time | Median delay |
|:-------------------|---------:|--------:|-------------:|
| Harbour – Skerry   |    1,512 |   87.9% |      1.4 min |
| Harbour – Lindholm |    1,020 |   95.2% |      0.3 min |
| Lindholm – Outer   |      888 |   93.8% |      0.6 min |

## A model of knock-on delay

If a vessel leaves late by $d_0$ minutes and each turnaround recovers $r$
minutes, the delay after $n$ rotations is

$$
d_n = \max\left(0,\; d_0 - n r\right) + \sum_{k=1}^{n} \varepsilon_k
$$ {#eq-knock-on}

where $\varepsilon_k$ is the fresh delay picked up on rotation $k$. With
$r \approx 1.5$ the Skerry evening rotations never catch up (@eq-knock-on).

::: {.callout-warning}
## Small samples
The Outer route runs only twice a day in winter. Treat its figures as
